analysis.one_liner: Taxes fund managers' performance pay as ordinary income instead of at the lower capital-gains rate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote — it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2019 and died there when the Congress ended, having drawn a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate funds take much of their pay as "carried interest," which is taxed at the long-term capital-gains rate (about 20%) instead of regular income rates (up to 37%), and the tax can be deferred until the fund sells its investments. This bill would treat that pay as ordinary income each year, subject to normal income tax and self-employment tax. It was introduced by the top Democrat on the tax-writing committee, sent to that committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways. First, the bill closes a tax break used almost exclusively by a small group of the highest-paid people in the country, so the tax burden they carry would grow while everyone else's would not. Second, closing the break would raise federal revenue, easing pressure to cut services or raise other taxes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the carried-interest concept: fund managers' performance-based pay would be taxed each year as ordinary income and subject to self-employment tax, instead of at the roughly 20% long-term capital-gains rate [S2].
It also ends the deferral benefit: under current law managers can put off paying tax on this pay until the fund itself realizes income, sometimes for years [S2].

The bill reaches the common workarounds — it covers managers' interests held through related entities and financial contracts tied to the fund, and it taxes pay financed by loans from the fund itself, closing a path managers used to take cash out without owing tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers, who would owe tax on their performance pay at rates up to 37% plus self-employment tax rather than the roughly 20% capital-gains rate, and would owe it annually rather than on deferral.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The bill's formula is complex: it calculates a manager's deemed pay from the fund's invested capital, the manager's share of profits, and a statutory interest rate, which would mean significant compliance work for firms and a heavy administrative load for the IRS [S3].

Defenders of the current treatment argue that carried interest rewards managers who tie up their own money and take long-term investment risk, and that taxing it as salary would discourage that activity; the bill also applies a 10-year lookback that recaptures tax when a manager sells out early, which its critics call punitive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a straightforward fairness fix: it taxes one form of executive pay the same way wages are taxed, and the people affected are nearly all at the very top of the income scale. The real weakness is design, not principle — the bill replaces a simple current-law rule with an elaborate formula and an aggressive anti-abuse apparatus, so enforcement would be a continuing contest between the IRS and well-funded tax planners.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden, joined by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, introduced the bill on May 23, 2019 [S3, S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the action record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
Only one senator, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill, and no Republican signed on [S4, S3].
Wyden was the ranking Democrat on the Finance Committee, meaning the bill's chief sponsor sat at the committee but in the minority, and the committee's Republican majority never brought it up [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers, who kept paying tax on their performance pay at the lower capital-gains rate and on deferral for another two years and beyond.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers who kept the tax break

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Industry whose carried-interest pay the bill would re-tax
against.what_they_did: The industry has waged a sustained lobbying campaign across multiple Congresses to preserve carried-interest treatment, and no Republican committee member supported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the bill's only cosponsor was a Democrat; the Republican-led Finance Committee took no action on it.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their signature form of pay — carried interest — would be taxed at ordinary income rates up to 37% plus self-employment tax instead of about 20%, and taxed annually rather than deferred. Their interest in keeping the break runs against ordinary taxpayers, who cover the revenue the break costs.

The bill explicitly lists real estate held for rental or investment among the assets whose managers' pay is re-taxed, so real estate fund sponsors lose the same break. Real estate interests are a traditional pillar of the carried-interest defense.
